subsection: 5. Case study: de Valera in America, June 1919–December 1920

notes.h: Case study: background and causes, 1916 to April 1919
notes.b: Éamon de Valera went to America in June 1919 as head of the Dáil government (the Irish republican parliament), after escaping from prison in England, to win recognition for the Irish Republic. To see why he was chosen and why he needed to go, start with the events that made him a leader.
points: De Valera was born in New York in 1882 to an Irish mother and a Spanish father and was raised in Co. Limerick, so he had a link to America that few Irish leaders had.

In the Easter Rising of 1916 he commanded the Volunteer garrison at Boland's Mill in Dublin. He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted to penal servitude (imprisonment with hard labour), so he survived to lead the movement afterwards.

Sinn Féin, the republican party that grew in strength after the Rising, won 73 of the 105 Irish seats in the general election of December 1918. Its MPs refused to sit at Westminster and instead met as Dáil Éireann.
The first Dáil met on 21 January 1919 and declared an Irish Republic. A republic that no other state recognised had little standing abroad, which is why recognition became the goal of the mission.
De Valera was arrested in May 1918 in the round-up that followed the so-called German Plot (the British claim that Sinn Féin was plotting with Germany), and he was held in Lincoln Gaol in England.

He escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919, in an escape arranged by Michael Collins and Harry Boland. Collins and Boland were close allies who each played a major part in the months that followed.
In April 1919 the Dáil elected him head of its ministry, as Príomh Aire, usually translated as President. This gave him the authority to speak for the Republic abroad.
notes.tip: Document questions can use extracts about the Lincoln escape and Collins's part in it, so know the date, 3 February 1919, and the names of Collins and Boland.

notes.h: Case study: why he went, the aims of the mission
notes.b: The mission had four aims, and each was shaped by what had already gone wrong at the Paris Peace Conference. Irish republicans had hoped the world's leaders would hear Ireland's case there, but they found the door closed.
points: Self-determination (the principle that each people should choose its own government) was promoted by US President Woodrow Wilson at the Paris Peace Conference. Irish republicans appealed to it because it seemed to support an independent Irish state.

The Dáil sent envoys to Paris, including Seán T. O'Kelly, but Wilson did not press Britain on Irish self-determination and the Irish delegates were not heard. This pushed the Dáil to turn to the American public instead.

An Irish Race Convention in Philadelphia in February 1919 sent three Irish-American delegates, Frank P. Walsh, Edward F. Dunne and Michael J. Ryan, to Paris to ask Wilson to hear Ireland's case. They later visited Ireland.

Irish America already had organisations to build on. The Friends of Irish Freedom, founded in 1916 and led by Judge Daniel Cohalan of New York and John Devoy, had supported Irish independence since then, so the ground was prepared.
Aim 1: to win US recognition of the Irish Republic, meaning that the American government would formally accept it as an independent state.
Aim 2: to raise funds for the Dáil government, which had no income of its own and was soon fighting a war.
Aim 3: to influence the 1920 US presidential election, so that the next president would back the Republic.
Aim 4: to put pressure on Britain, because American sympathy for Ireland would embarrass its wartime ally.
notes.tip: Aims are asked directly. A clear list of recognition, funds, influence on Paris and the 1920 election, and pressure on Britain earns easy marks, and strong answers then judge each aim in turn.

notes.h: Case study: the arrival and the first appearance, June 1919
notes.b: De Valera had to leave Britain in secret because he was an escaped prisoner. His arrival in America was prepared in advance and launched his public campaign.
points: He left Britain secretly on a ship from Liverpool as a stowaway, so that British officials would not catch him. He reached the USA in June 1919.
Harry Boland had already gone ahead to prepare the way, arranging contacts and meetings with Irish-American organisations so that de Valera could start work at once.
On 6 June 1919 the US Senate passed a resolution asking the Peace Conference to hear Irish representatives. It showed sympathy but did not commit the American government to anything.
His first public appearance in New York came in late June 1919, and he stayed at the Waldorf-Astoria hotel. This launched the tour of the cities with the largest Irish communities.
notes.tip: Give only the Liverpool stowaway passage and the June 1919 arrival. Do not say he left Ireland secretly in May. Document questions on his reception may mention a hotel, so link the Waldorf-Astoria to New York in June 1919.

notes.h: Case study: the tour and its reception, 1919 to 1920
notes.b: De Valera toured the cities where Irish Americans were most numerous, and they greeted him as the head of a nation. The crowds were large, but the American government and press were more guarded.
points: On 29 June 1919 he addressed a huge rally at Fenway Park in Boston. His meetings in other cities such as Chicago and New York also drew large Irish-American crowds, who gave him receptions, parades and donations.

The tour continued through 1919 and into 1920, and he also visited Irish communities in western states. Irish-American organisations and parishes arranged his meetings, and local branches raised money and sent subscriptions to Dublin.
He was given honours as well as welcomes. He was given the title of chief of the Chippewa nation and presents of beaded work, an example of how warmly he was received.
His message was always the same: recognition of the Republic, support for the Dáil, and funds for the struggle in Ireland.
The reception was enthusiastic among Irish Americans. The American government and most of the press treated the mission with caution.
British officials objected to the tour, which they regarded as propaganda against British rule in Ireland.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for the tour with Fenway Park, so give the place, the city and the date, 29 June 1919. Document questions may show crowds, a parade or honours such as the Chippewa title, so say what that shows about his reception. Do not give an exact crowd size.

notes.h: Case study: funds and the Dáil bond drive
notes.b: Money was the aim the mission came closest to achieving. The Dáil government needed funds to run a state and support a war.
points: The Dáil authorised a loan, and bond certificates were sold to Irish Americans in a campaign launched in the USA in January 1920. Supporters could thus invest in the struggle for independence.
The target was five million dollars, and about that sum had been raised by 1921, though sources differ on the exact total. Say 'about', never 'exactly'.
The drive used the networks of Irish-American organisations, parishes and clubs to reach donors in cities across the United States.
Disputes arose over who controlled the money, and Irish-American leaders disagreed with de Valera about how the funds should be spent.

The bond drive in the USA must not be confused with the National Loan raised in Ireland by Michael Collins as Minister for Finance. Together they gave the Dáil government a financial base at home and in the diaspora (Irish people living abroad).
Francis M. Carroll's study of the Dáil loans and their finances, Money for Ireland (2002), stresses the importance of the money for the Republic's finances.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for the bond drive and its outcome, so give January 1920, the five million dollar target and the result of about that sum by 1921. Document questions on bonds need only what the extract shows plus the context, that these were Dáil bonds for the Republic.

notes.h: Case study: the conflict with Irish-American leaders
notes.b: De Valera's mission divided Irish America, and his clash with Devoy and Judge Cohalan weakened the unity of the movement. It was a quarrel over who was in charge.
points: John Devoy and Judge Daniel Cohalan led the Friends of Irish Freedom, which had supported Irish independence since 1916. Devoy edited the Gaelic American, a newspaper founded in 1903.
They quarrelled with de Valera over the control of funds and of the American movement, and the quarrel was carried out in the press.

Devoy and Cohalan saw de Valera as trying to take control of an organisation they had built. De Valera wanted an organisation that answered to the Dáil, so the dispute was about Dáil authority against American independence.
Harry Boland, who had prepared the American side of the mission, backed de Valera, and the two camps traded accusations in the Gaelic American and other papers.
The split reduced the unity of Irish America. De Valera turned to a new organisation of his own, a rival to the Friends of Irish Freedom.
The quarrel showed the difficulty of running a movement from America when the leaders in Ireland had their own priorities.
notes.tip: Controversy questions need the Devoy and Cohalan quarrel, the money disputes and the Cuba interview, each with a short explanation of why it was controversial. For the quarrel, say it was over control of funds and of the movement.

notes.h: Case study: the Westminster Gazette interview, February 1920
notes.b: De Valera's own public statements caused controversy among his supporters. In February 1920 he suggested a compromise that many republicans found hard to accept.
points: In February 1920 an interview with de Valera appeared in the Westminster Gazette, a British newspaper. In it he suggested that Britain's security fears could be met by treating Ireland as the United States treated Cuba.

Cuba was a state that accepted limits on its foreign policy, in effect American influence, while remaining independent. The Cuba analogy therefore offered Britain a guarantee against Ireland becoming a base for its enemies.
The comparison caused controversy among republicans at home and abroad, who felt it offered a compromise on full independence.
Cohalan and Devoy used the interview to attack him.
De Valera himself argued that he was only showing American opinion that the Irish demand was reasonable.
notes.tip: Say the interview appeared in the Westminster Gazette, not that he gave it in London, because he was in the USA. Explain why it was controversial: it seemed to accept less than full independence.

notes.h: Case study: the 1920 conventions and the presidential election
notes.b: In 1920 de Valera tried to win a commitment to recognition from both major American parties, because the next president would decide whether the USA recognised the Republic. Neither party gave one.
points: The Republican National Convention met in Chicago in June 1920, and the Democratic National Convention met in San Francisco in June and July 1920. Do not mix up the two cities.
De Valera approached delegates and party leaders at both conventions, seeking a plank (a policy commitment in the party platform) recognising the Irish Republic.
The Republican platform ignored the request, and the Democrats adopted only a resolution of sympathy with Irish aspirations for self-government. Sympathy was not recognition.
The Republican candidate Warren G. Harding won the presidential election in November 1920, and his administration did not recognise the Republic.

Irish-American anger at the Wilson administration's refusal to back Irish self-determination hurt the Democrats in November 1920. Neither Wilson nor Harding recognised the Republic, and neither party backed it.
notes.tip: Strong answers judge the aim of influencing the election as not achieved, with the dates June 1920 and November 1920. Say Irish-American anger hurt the Democrats, without giving percentages.

notes.h: Case study: the AARIR and rising American sympathy, late 1920
notes.b: After the failure at the conventions the campaign was reorganised. At the same time, events in Ireland increased sympathy in America.
points: The American Association for the Recognition of the Irish Republic (AARIR) was founded in November 1920 as de Valera's own campaigning body. The Friends of Irish Freedom continued, so the AARIR became a rival to them for de Valera's supporters.
The new association grew rapidly and claimed several hundred thousand members, and it organised rallies and lobbied members of Congress. Do not give an exact membership figure, because sources vary.
Terence MacSwiney, Lord Mayor of Cork, died on hunger strike on 25 October 1920. His death received wide American press coverage and helped the Irish cause.

An American Commission on Conditions in Ireland was set up in late 1920 to investigate British reprisals in Ireland and increased American sympathy. It was a separate body and was not run by the AARIR.
notes.tip: Document questions on the founding of the AARIR need only what the extract shows plus the context. Keep the Friends of Irish Freedom (1916, Devoy and Cohalan) and the AARIR (November 1920, de Valera) clearly apart.

notes.h: Case study: events in Ireland while he was away
notes.b: While de Valera was in America, the Anglo-Irish War (the guerrilla war between the IRA and British forces) intensified. Events at home affected how Americans saw the mission and how the Dáil was run.
points: The Soloheadbeg ambush on 21 January 1919 marked the start of the Anglo-Irish War, which lasted until 1921.
The British government banned the Dáil on 12 September 1919, and its ministers went underground.
Michael Collins, as Minister for Finance and director of IRA intelligence, ran much of the war in Ireland while de Valera was in America.

From March 1920 the British government reinforced the Royal Irish Constabulary (the police) with the Black and Tans and, from July 1920, the Auxiliaries. Reprisals against civilians were widely reported in American newspapers, which helped the Irish cause.
Kevin Barry, an 18-year-old IRA Volunteer, was hanged in Dublin on 1 November 1920.

On 21 November 1920, known as Bloody Sunday, IRA gunmen killed British officers and agents in Dublin, and British forces then fired on a crowd at Croke Park, killing 14. This is not the Bloody Sunday of 1972.
Auxiliaries burned part of Cork city in December 1920.

The Government of Ireland Act, passed in December 1920, created separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland. De Valera returned to Ireland in December 1920, and Harry Boland stayed on in America.
notes.tip: Give dates for these events and say only what affected the mission, such as reprisals reported in the American press. Say he returned in December 1920 and give no more exact date.

notes.b: The mission secured publicity and money for the Republic, but not the recognition its leaders wanted. Its results were mixed, and they cost the movement something too.
points: No American government recognised the Irish Republic during the mission or in the years that followed. This was the main aim, so its failure is the central fact in any judgement.
The mission raised money for the Dáil government, which helped to pay for the war and the Dáil's administration.
The mission raised the profile of the Irish Republic in American newspapers and at public meetings, so Americans heard the Irish case directly.
The split among Irish-American organisations weakened the Friends of Irish Freedom and led to a new body, the AARIR.

De Valera was away for about eighteen months, from June 1919 to December 1920. His absence left the Dáil government without its president at a time of war, and relations between him and Collins were strained.
The mission was one of the first major efforts by the Irish Republic to win international recognition, and it shows both the possibilities and the limits of diaspora politics.
Harry Boland remained in the United States after de Valera left, and the AARIR carried on the campaign into 1921.
notes.tip: Examiners ask whether his aims were achieved. Judge each in turn: recognition not achieved, funds achieved, election influence not achieved, publicity achieved.

notes.h: Assessment: success or failure in America
notes.b: Whether the mission succeeded depends on which aim you judge. It won money and publicity but lost the recognition it was meant to win.
points: Achievement: the mission brought the Irish Republic's case to large American audiences and raised about five million dollars for the Dáil government, which paid for the war and the Dáil's administration.
Limit: neither the Wilson administration nor the Harding administration recognised the Republic, and neither party backed it. The Irish-American movement was divided by the mission.
Aims achieved: funds and publicity. Aims not achieved: recognition and influence on the 1920 election.
Other costs: de Valera's long absence from Ireland, about eighteen months, and strained relations with Collins.

Contemporary view: supporters called the mission a triumph, while Devoy, Cohalan and other Irish-American critics resented his attempt to control the movement, and the British government and its allies called it dangerous and divisive.
Contemporary view in Ireland: some nationalists argued that the time spent in America would have been better used at home.

Later view: historians stress that the mission was a propaganda and fundraising success but a diplomatic failure, because the recognition it sought was never granted. Carroll's study stresses the importance of the money.
notes.tip: Higher Level essays ask how successful the mission was or whether his aims were achieved. Give a stated judgement supported by paired points, money and publicity against no recognition, and large crowds against a split Irish America.

keyTerms.definition: The bond certificates sold to Irish Americans from 1920 to raise money for the Dáil government and the struggle for independence.
The formal acceptance by a foreign government of the Irish Republic as an independent state, which the Dáil sought from the United States.

keyTerms.term: American Association for the Recognition of the Irish Republic
keyTerms.definition: An American campaigning body founded in November 1920 to press for US recognition of the Irish Republic.
An Irish-American organisation founded in 1916 and led by Judge Daniel Cohalan, which split with de Valera during his American mission.
The assembly of elected representatives that claimed to be the parliament of the Irish Republic from 1919.
The conflict of 1919 to 1921 between the IRA and British forces, which ran alongside de Valera's American mission.
The Act passed in December 1920 that created separate parliaments for Northern and Southern Ireland.
The principle, associated with President Wilson, that peoples should choose their own governments; Irish republicans invoked it at Paris and in America.
